new_statements.quote: [p. 94, sec. 3.5 STRESS] Primary stress in PSB occurs regularly on the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word, reconstructed on the basis of its reflex on the penult in all SB languages except in predictable environments in NB. This observation applies to words, not merely to stems, so that suffixation results in the shift of stress to the right. Example from CS.2: bónoq 'to kill'; amónoq 'kills'; bonóqun 'kill it'; pagbonóqbi 'your act of fighting together'; pagbonoqánbi 'the cause of your fighting together'. [p. 277, Appendix I] Note that stress in all Sama-Bajaw languages falls on the penult, with rare exceptions which are indicated.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (Gault 1979:54, StressTyp2) has strict penultimate stress with suffixation moving stress to the right; Pallesen 1985:94 states exactly this for all Sama-Bajaw languages (penult of the word, suffixation shifts stress right) and p. 164 adds that word stress is predictable (non-phonemic) in all SB daughter languages. The statement is family-wide (example from CS.2 Sama Dilaut), not a Balangingi-specific description, but Balangingiq (NS.1/2/4/8) is among the data languages and no exception is flagged for it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-contrastive) and falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word in Proto-Sama-Bajaw and in all Sama-Bajaw daughter languages, which includes the Northern Sulu group to which Balangingi(q) belongs; the domain is the whole word including suffixes and enclitics, so suffixation shifts stress rightward onto the new penult (bónoq, bonóqun, pagbonoqánbi). The only systematic exception Pallesen states is for NB (Sabah Land Bajaw = West Coast Bajau), where a schwa penult pushes stress to the ultima; no exception is indicated for any NS/Balangingiq variety.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (only primary stress is discussed).
new_statements.exceptions: NB (Sabah Land Bajaw) only: 'In NB stress occurs on the penult except when the vowel of the penult is the mid central vowel /ə/, in which case it occurs on the ultima', with degemination (PSB *bə́lli 'to buy' > bəlí NB.1). Appendix I: 'rare exceptions which are indicated' (i.e. marked on individual cited forms); none concern Balangingi. Not an exception but context: Sulu Tausug lost phonemic stress through convergence with Sulu Sama (sec. 5.1.3, 7.4.6.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Pallesen's statement is family-level (PSB and 'all SB languages'; worked example from CS.2 Sama Dilaut = Central Sama), not a dedicated description of Balangingi; Balangingi appears as the Northern Sulu (NS) group: NS.1 Tagtabun Balangingiq, NS.2 Tongquil Balangingiq, NS.4 Panigayan Balangingiq (data from Diment and Gault, i.e. the same fieldworkers as the catalog source Gault 1979), NS.8 Kawit Balangingiq; SIL catalogs the monograph under Central Sama [sml].

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict penultimate (penultimate stress) with word domain rests on Gault 1979 §1.3 p. 54, a dedicated phonemics article on exactly this variety; the quotation is verified verbatim in the text and PDF we hold ( page 60 = printed p. 54), and the same article independently uses penultimate stress as a syllable-count diagnostic (§1.4.2) and states that suffixes/enclitic pronouns shift stress rightward while monosyllabic particles are extrametrical — all consistent with the record. Glottolog's other descriptive items are morphosyntax/discourse (Gault 1999 held, silent on stress), and Ingilan's field survey confirms no grammar or other phonology of Bangingi exists, so the best available source is.
